why: A population claim about awards ('most') with no source. Some awards have substitution clauses for weekend holidays, so this needs checking against the award data or rewording to cite a specific award.

claim: 'Most reductions were processed before the end of 2025 ... The ATO has since confirmed processing is complete for all study and training support debts' (key facts line 21: 'Complete as of 2026').
why: None of the page's three sources is an ATO completion notice (they are Study Assist, Department of Education FAQs and a ministerial release). This needs an ATO or Study Assist source with a date.

claim: The marginal tax rate on $90,000 is {TAX_BRACKETS[2].rate}% plus the 2% Medicare levy.
why: The 2% Medicare levy is hard-coded rather than taken from the constant. The bracket is picked by index [2] rather than looked up by income. Both are correct for 2026-27 but fragile.

claim: Under casual conversion the employer can only refuse on fair and reasonable operational grounds.
why: Under the employee choice pathway (Fair Work Act s 66F) the employer can also refuse when the employee still meets the definition of a casual employee, or when conversion would break a recruitment or selection law. 'Only on operational grounds' is too narrow, and the FAQ on the same page says 'limited grounds' (faqs.ts line 31).

claim: Different pathways applied to some casuals up to 26 August 2025; the Fair Work Ombudsman explains the transitional rules.
why: lib/constants/casual-conversion.ts records something different: eligible casuals employed before 26 August 2024 could first give notice from 26 February 2025 (not a small business) or 26 August 2025 (small business). The FAQ suggests a different pathway applied until that date, which the recorded source does not say. Check the wording against FWO's transitional rules.

claim: The salary table shows ranges 'including base salary and common overtime'
why: This contradicts the methodology note at line 225, which says the ranges include base rate and typical allowances 'but excluding overtime'. One of the two is wrong. The 'well above the national average' claim on the same line also cites no source.

claim: nextIncrease: null, verifiedOn 28 August 2026, rates 'as of December 2025' with the 2023 agreement's increases exhausted.
why: This may be stale. The last increase under the 2023 agreement was in December 2025. A successor WA teachers' agreement or a new increase date may have been registered since the 28 August 2026 check.

claim: Casual penalty = permanent percentage plus the 25% casual loading (Schedule B.2.1; cl 11.2).
why: The note cites cl 11.2 for the casual loading, but LOCAL_GOVERNMENT_AWARD.meta.casualLoadingClause (line 837) is 'cl 11.1'. One of the two clause citations may be wrong. Check against the MA000112 award text.

claim: Every bonus dollar sits in your top bracket: 30%, 37% or 45%, because your salary has already used up the tax-free threshold and the lower brackets.
why: The list leaves out the 15% bracket that applies in 2026-27 for income between $18,201 and $45,000. A payee whose salary plus bonus stays under $45,000 has a 15% marginal rate. The rates are also typed into the string rather than taken from the tax-rate constants.

claim: The tax saving ranges from $150 per $1,000 sacrificed (at the 30% bracket) to $300 per $1,000 (at the 45% bracket)
why: The figures are typed in by hand and leave out the 15% bracket, where the saving is nil, as well as the Medicare levy. The range should be derived from the bracket constants and CONTRIBUTIONS_TAX_RATE.

claim: residents benefit from the $0 tax-free threshold
why: The resident tax-free threshold is $18,200 (taxed at 0%), not $0. The intended wording is probably 'the 0% rate on the $18,200 tax-free threshold'. I left it because changing it would change a number.

claim: only the extra income is taxed at the higher rate, so a raise never cuts your take-home pay
why: raiseOutcome() in lib/constants/marginal-rates.ts includes Medicare levy surcharge cliffs when the 'No private hospital cover' box is ticked. Crossing an MLS tier charges the surcharge on the whole income, so netGain can be negative and the note would then claim the opposite of the figure above it. 'never' is also a brand-forbidden word for tax advice.

claim: a raise never lowers your take-home pay
why: The Medicare levy surcharge is charged on the whole income from $105,001 for a single without private hospital cover (line 135 of the same page says so). A $1 raise from $105,000 to $105,001 adds about $1,050 of surcharge, so take-home pay falls. The claim holds only with private hospital cover. The same claim appears in the FAQ (see next item).

claim: Business deductions from gig work can only be offset against your gig income (or total income if you are a sole trader reporting in your individual tax return).
why: This reads as self-contradictory: a gig worker is a sole trader reporting in their individual return. It also leaves out the non-commercial loss rules, which decide whether a business loss can be offset against wage income.

claim: Where both spouses would otherwise be liable and one is in a Category 1 exemption category, a signed family agreement decides which of you claims the full exemption and which claims the half.
why: The condition reads oddly. If only one spouse is in Category 1, the other has no exemption to split. The ATO family agreement (QC27036) seems to apply when both spouses qualify for an exemption and have dependants. Check the wording against the ATO page.

page: radiologist / anaesthetist / surgeon salary pages (public hospital section, NSW)
claim: NSW staff specialist rates are interim (IB2026_006, from 1 July 2025) and the Staff Specialists (State) Award is before the NSW IRC
why: The source is dated 20 January 2026 and was read 9 October 2026. If the NSW IRC has since decided, the interim rates and the 'before the NSW IRC' statement are stale.

claim: Brisbane March 2026 inflation was 4.2%, above the 3% increase, but the rates shown are before any CPI uplift.
why: By the note's own logic the capped 0.5% uplift (cl 6.1(b)) has been triggered. The QLD_2025 and QLD_2026 tables, the headline and the FAQ figures may therefore understate current teacher aide pay by up to 0.5%. The department's uplifted table should be checked for.

claim: work-related expenses, salary sacrifice contributions, or the "Low Income Tax Offset" reduce your assessable income below the projected amount
why: LITO is a tax offset. It reduces tax payable, not assessable income. Salary sacrifice reduces assessable salary but is not a tax deduction, so the item lumps three different mechanisms together under 'Significant tax deductions'.

claim: The $80,000 worked example: excess $10,472, repayment about $1,571, $30/week STSL (about $1,560) 'within a few dollars'.
why: If the tax-time year is corrected to FY2025-26 ($67,000 threshold), the excess becomes $13,000 and the repayment about $1,950. The $30/week STSL figure would then no longer reconcile, so the whole example has to be recomputed from constants, not patched.

claim: Probably not. Sole traders, partnerships and trusts without a company trustee are generally in the WA state system.
why: The state-system paragraph at line 109 and the standfirst at line 14 say definitely that sole traders and unincorporated partnerships are in the WA state system. The FAQ hedges the same rule with 'Probably not' and 'generally'. Check the WA Government 'Which system of employment law applies' source and either make the answer definite or name the specific exception.

claim: If contracting pays 30%+ more than the equivalent employee salary, the financial benefit usually outweighs the loss of entitlements.
why: This is an unsourced rule of thumb written like a rule. It also conflicts with the calculator's 'Value Equivalent required approx.' figure, which uses a 1.15 multiplier (contractor-vs-employee-calculator.tsx line 44). The AUDIT does not mark this page for labelled editorial judgment, so I left it as it is.

claim: Schedule G translation rates affect home care aged-care employees covered on or before 31 December 2024
why: Date is typed into prose, not taken from a constant. It should come from the same source as the SCHADS_UNVERIFIED notes.

claim: Under Payday Super contributions should land within roughly a fortnight of each payday
why: The deadline is SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current.businessDaysToPay (7 business days), which is about 9 to 11 calendar days. It is 20 business days (about four weeks) for new employees or a new fund. 'Roughly a fortnight' overstates the standard deadline and understates the extended one. Consider rendering the business-day constants here instead.

claim: The ATO's Australian zone list was last updated on 1 July 2026. Darwin is Zone A.
why: This hard-coded date and placement do not appear in the constants file. Its source header lists only QC106871, QC105018 and QC106872, all retrieved 28 July 2026. Confirm the zone-list update date and Darwin's zone against the ATO Australian zone list and record the source.

claim: If you switch jobs, a delay in fund details 'can flow through to the 7-business-day deadline for your first contribution'.
why: The sibling article (payday-super-starts-july-2026.tsx line 30) says there is a longer window for some new employees while their fund details are confirmed. The two pages contradict each other on the new-employee deadline. The longer new-employee window under the payday super rules should be checked and one wording used on both pages.

claim: Occupancy expenses are only deductible if you have a dedicated home office used exclusively or primarily for work, and you run a business from home.
why: The ATO test is that the home is your principal place of business and an area is set aside exclusively for business activities. 'or primarily' looks too loose.

claim: From 1 September 2027, Level 2, Band 1, Increment 1 goes to $89,043
why: Low priority. $86,877 x 1.025 = $89,049, while Increment 7 ($107,514 to $110,201) matches 2.5% exactly. The gap is probably rounding in the QAS fortnightly schedule, but please check it against the updated Schedule 1.

claim: Salary packaging reduces your taxable income ... resulting in less tax withheld and a higher net monthly deposit.
why: Salary sacrifice to super or a novated lease reduces tax withheld, but the net deposit in your bank account goes down, not up, because the sacrificed amount leaves your pay before it lands. The gain is in total value (net pay plus the packaged benefit), not in the deposit. This answer also feeds FAQPage JSON-LD.

The figures check out against nurses-award-2020.ts today, but they are typed and not derived from the scale data, so they will go stale at the next Annual Wage Review. The enrolled nurse FAQ in the same file already derives its figures.

claim: union and professional association fees are fully deductible, including ... medical registration boards
why: Practitioner registration fees (for example AHPRA) are deductible, but they are not membership fees for a union or association. 'Fully deductible' also ignores any part of a fee that is not work-related.

claim: Your cost base for shares is what you paid plus brokerage and stamp duty on both the purchase and the sale.
why: No Australian state or territory charges stamp duty on transfers of listed (ASX) shares, so stamp duty on both the purchase and the sale looks wrong for the usual share sale. It could only apply to some unlisted-share transfers. The same answer also types '12 months' as a literal instead of using CGT_MINIMUM_OWNERSHIP_MONTHS.

claim: Unbilled time, insurance and sick days are why many contractors charge 1.4 to 1.6 times the employee rate.
why: This is a population claim with no source ('many contractors'). The same 1.4 to 1.6 rule of thumb appears at line 95. It is the lead of the 'What Rate Should I Charge?' section and is also in the FAQPage schema.

claim: NES notice periods (1 to 4 weeks, plus 1 if over 45)
why: Under the NES (Fair Work Act s117(3)(b)), the extra week applies only if the employee is over 45 AND has completed at least 2 years of continuous service with the employer. The meta description drops the 2-year service condition. The string is locked metadata, so I left it alone. Consider rewording within the length limit, for example 'plus 1 if over 45 with 2+ years' service'.

claim: An adult Subway sandwich artist ... must be paid at least $27.81 an hour ... from 1 July 2026.
why: ratesEffectiveFrom says 'the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026', but this FAQ answer says plain '1 July 2026'. It is a small precision mismatch on a date condition.

claim: Casual conversion pathway changes ... convert to permanent employment after 12 months (listed as a FY2026-27 change)
why: This conflicts with line 304: the employee choice pathway has applied since 26 August 2024, after 6 months (12 months for a small business employer). It is also not a FY2026-27 change. Line 331 (Right to Disconnect, August 2024 and August 2025) is also listed as a FY2026-27 change but is older.

claim: Standfirst: 'Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays nearly everywhere; Easter Saturday and Easter Sunday are not.'
why: This contradicts the same page's directAnswer and FAQ. Those say Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays in every state, Easter Saturday is a holiday in six jurisdictions, and Easter Sunday is a holiday everywhere except Tasmania. The standfirst should probably say 'in every state and territory' and that Easter Saturday and Easter Sunday are holidays in some states only. I left it unchan

claim: GST registration is mandatory once annual turnover exceeds $75,000 (also 'above $75,000' at 352 and 478).
why: The ATO test is a GST turnover of $75,000 or more, not more than $75,000. This is a boundary-wording issue.

claim: Apprentices in priority trades 'may receive $5,000–$10,000 in direct payments' under the Australian Apprenticeships Incentive System
why: This is a government program amount with no source, no date and no constant. The program changed from 1 July 2024 and 1 July 2025 (Key Apprenticeship Program), so it needs checking against the current DEWR settings.

claim: Employer-provided education that is sufficiently connected to the employee's current role is an exempt benefit.
why: Work-related education is usually brought to nil taxable value through the otherwise deductible rule, not listed as an exempt benefit. Check the label against the ATO FBT guide before it is repeated.

claim: Enrolled Nurse in Training (75% of Nurse 1) $53,523; Registered Nurse/Midwife in Training (75% of Nurse 2) $60,501.
why: 75% of Nurse 1.1 ($71,359) is $53,519 and 75% of Nurse 2.1 ($80,665) is $60,499. Both stored figures are $2 to $4 higher. That may be the agreement's own rounding or an earlier base compounded, but the labels claim exact 75%.

claim: Your employer's contribution must now reach your fund within 7 business days of each payday.
why: The 7-business-day Payday Super deadline is typed into the prose instead of coming from SUPER_GUARANTEE. That breaks the file's own rule that 'nothing is typed as a literal'. Move it to a constant and check it against the ATO's Payday Super guidance.

claim: the second income tax rate fell from 16% to 15% on 1 July 2026, so most taxpayers pay slightly less tax
why: 'Most taxpayers' is a claim about how many people are affected, with no source on the page. The 16% and 15% rates are typed in by hand rather than taken from the tax bracket constants.

claim: Deductions reduce your assessable income, which reduces tax payable.
why: Deductions reduce taxable income (assessable income minus deductions), not assessable income. The WATO page on the same site says 'A deduction lowers your taxable income'. Left unchanged because it is a terminology/fact correction.

claim: Parenting Payment Single recipients keep the Pensioner Concession Card for 12 weeks after the payment ends.
why: The condition seems to be missing. The extension applies when PPS stops because of employment income, not whenever it ends. The sentence before it does state its condition ('suspended because you are working').

claim: The tax benefit of super "could be 22% to 32% per dollar for those in the 37% or 45% brackets" (repeated as "22 to 32 cents per dollar" at line 145).
why: The range is internally inconsistent. 22 is 37% minus 15% without Medicare, and 32 is 45% plus the 2% Medicare levy minus 15%. It should be either 22 to 30 cents (no Medicare) or 24 to 32 cents (with Medicare).

claim: Submit a new TFN declaration when you take on or pay off a HECS debt, change your tax-free threshold claim or change residency (also the table 'How to Fix' cells at lines 149, 154, 164 and 169).
why: For changes with the same payer the ATO uses a withholding declaration (NAT 3093), not a new TFN declaration. Line 127 on the same page already says to give a 'withholding declaration' once the debt is repaid, so the page contradicts itself. Table cells and headings are locked.

claim: Column 2: withholding does not start until your weekly earnings pass about {formatAUD(362)}
why: The figure is typed into the page as formatAUD(362) and is not computed. Running calculatePAYGWithholding(g, 'weekly') for 2026-27 gives $0 withheld for every amount from $358 to $364 and $1 at $365. So withholding starts above $364, not $362. The $362 may be left over from the 2025-26 table.

claim: Table caption: "including the 2% Medicare levy" (the methodology text at line 334 also says "the 2% Medicare levy")
why: The 2% is typed into the JSX, not read from code. It will drift if the levy changes. The prose should render it from the levy constant.

claim: grosses ${formatAUD(DAY_RATE_GROSS)} over 48 working weeks
why: The figure 48 is typed into the prose and into DAY_RATE_GROSS (line 33: 1_000 * 5 * 48). BILLABLE_WEEKS = 48 already exists in the same file. If BILLABLE_WEEKS changes, the prose and this number will drift apart.

claim: 'only the first {maxContributionBaseAnnual} of salary counts (the maximum contribution base)' and, in tax-on-salary.tsx, 'capped at the {maxContributionBaseAnnual} maximum contribution base'
why: The ATO sets the maximum super contribution base per quarter ($62,500 a quarter, per entity-attribute-analysis.md). The site shows the annualised figure under the bare label 'maximum contribution base', so a reader checking the ATO's figure will see a different number. Consider the wording 'the annual equivalent of the quarterly maximum contribution base'. Constant: SUPER_GUARANTEE.maxContribution

claim: each additional dollar of gross pay is taxed at a higher marginal rate; net corresponds to a gross of approximately $1,500 (or $78,000 per year)
why: Under progressive rates, only income above each bracket threshold is taxed at the higher rate, not every extra dollar. $1,500 is exact, not approximate, because example1500 is worked out from 1_500, and $1,500 and $78,000 are typed in rather than rendered with formatAUD.

claim: Turning 60 before 30 June moves the rate from 32% to 17%.
why: Correct today, but the 60 is typed into the text while the same file imports PRESERVATION_AGE. The caption at line 126 ('Preservation age is 60 for anyone born after 30 June 1964') also types the age instead of using the constant.

claim: Services Australia uses ATI for Family Tax Benefit, childcare subsidies 'and other income-tested payments'
why: Income support payments such as JobSeeker use the social security ordinary income test, not adjusted taxable income. Only FTB and Child Care Subsidy clearly use ATI.

claim: Most PAYG employees owed a refund can lodge late without a penalty
why: Population claim with no figure. It also reads as more certain than the ATO rule it follows from, which says the ATO 'generally' will not issue the notice. Consider 'A PAYG employee owed a refund generally will not be charged the penalty...'.

claim: Employees with 12 months' service can request flexible arrangements if they are a parent, carer, over 55, experiencing domestic violence, or have a disability.
why: The NES list since the 6 June 2023 Secure Jobs Better Pay changes also covers pregnant employees and people supporting a family or household member who is experiencing family and domestic violence. The NES term is 'family and domestic violence'. The list looks incomplete.

claim: Division 293 'doubles the tax' on contributions from the base rate to the combined rate.
why: This is true only for the part of the contributions Division 293 applies to (the lesser of the contributions or the excess over the threshold). I reworded it to 'the contributions it applies to'. Please confirm the wording against the ATO Division 293 page.

claim: The employer cannot simply stop offering shifts to avoid providing notice or redundancy pay if the worker has conversion rights.
why: Casuals have no NES notice or redundancy entitlement. The actual protection under the Fair Work Act (s66L) stops an employer from ending employment or cutting hours to avoid the casual's right to change to permanent employment. The current wording misstates what the protection is.

claim: The only difference during probation is that the notice period for termination is typically shorter (usually 1 week).
why: The NES notice period depends on length of service (1 week under 1 year), not on probation. The main legal effect of probation is the unfair dismissal minimum employment period (6 months, or 12 months for a small business). 'The only difference' looks wrong.

claim: Compulsory repayments stop once the balance is zero (original said this 'immediately' boosts take-home pay); also 'compulsory repayment percentage applied to your income'
why: An employer keeps withholding HELP amounts until you update your withholding declaration, and amounts already withheld come back at tax time, so 'immediately' was wrong. I removed it. Also, since 2025-26 the repayment uses a marginal system on income above the threshold, so 'percentage applied to your income' may need to say 'repayment rate'.

claim: Long service leave ... 8.67 weeks after 10 years ... about 1.67% of the base salary ... For a $100,000 employee, this adds approximately $1,670 per year. Employers must accrue this liability on their balance sheet from the employee's start date.
why: All the figures are typed, not derived. The 'must accrue from start date' claim comes from an accounting standard (AASB 119 for reporting entities), not an employment law rule for every employer. The VIC and ACT schemes (about 6.07 weeks after 7 years) and the SA and NT schemes (13 weeks after 10 years) differ.

claim: The ATO will review your objection and issue a decision, typically within 60 days.
why: The ATO's published service standard for finalising objections is 56 days (after it has all the information it needs). 60 days is the period after which a taxpayer can give notice requiring a decision. The two are different things, and the figure is hardcoded.

claim: Working one of these attracts public holiday penalty rates under most awards.
why: 'most awards' is an unsourced population claim.

claim: The annual concessional contributions cap is $30,000.
why: Hard-coded in prose and not taken from a constant. The cap is indexed, so it needs checking against the ATO for 2026-27, the year the page's tax table uses.

claim: On $80,000 a resident pays about $14,520 in income tax and $1,600 Medicare levy in 2026-27, leaving about $63,880 a year, or $1,228 a week
why: The figures check out for 2026-27 (15% first bracket), but they are hard-coded in the FAQ and JSON-LD, so they go stale when rates change. Generate them with calculatePayBreakdown({grossSalary: 80000}). The same applies to the $1,571 HELP figure at line 56.

claim: Money is 'locked until preservation age (currently 60)'.
why: 60 is typed into JSX here. The FAQ file derives preservation age from PRESERVATION_AGE_TABLE, so this copy can drift from that constant.

claim: 'If your employer contributes $12,000 in SG, you can salary sacrifice up to {formatAUD(CAP - 12_000)}'
why: The $12,000 SG example is typed with no link to the SG rate or a salary. It is fine as an illustration, but it should be derived (for example, the SG rate times an example salary) so it stays consistent if the cap or the SG rate changes.

claim: You can change the percentage online twice a financial year.
why: As far as I know, Services Australia lets families change their CCS withholding percentage at any time in their online account, with no twice-a-year limit. Needs checking against the Services Australia CCS withholding page.

claim: Centrelink withholds tax at a rate you choose (or a default rate)
why: Services Australia does not withhold tax from JobSeeker, Youth Allowance or Age Pension by default. Tax is withheld only if the recipient asks for a voluntary tax deduction, so '(or a default rate)' looks wrong. 'issues a Centrelink Payment Summary' may also need checking: the statement is now supplied through myGov and pre-filled to the ATO.

claim: The same Act adds a new offset on top of the rate cut. The Working Australians Tax Offset pays $250 against tax from 2027-28
why: Here "the same Act" means LEGISLATED_CUT_2027_28.act, the Treasury Laws Amendment (More Cost of Living Relief) Act 2025. But lib/constants/tax-2027-28.ts (lines 15-27, 58) says the WATO comes from the Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026, assented 26 June 2026. The ATO also describes the WATO as a non-refundable maximum benefit of $250, so "pays $250" overstates it. It should say "u

claim: the same gross salary is worth more in the APS than in the VPS once the 15.4% employer superannuation contribution is counted
why: 15.4% is the APS median employer contribution (aps.ts:402-404, and the table on this page says '15.4% (median)'). The prose states it as the APS contribution without 'median'.

claim: NSW, South Australia and Tasmania set no minimum age; Victoria and Queensland set 13 ...; Western Australia and the Northern Territory restrict ...
why: Hard-coded list duplicates MINIMUM_WORKING_AGE (line 94 uses the computed noMinimum instead). Both FAQ 4 and FAQ 5 omit the ACT, whose data summary is 'No minimum age stated; hours capped by age'.

claim: ECM break-even is above the ${formatPercent(0.47, 0)} top rate including the Medicare levy
why: 0.47 is typed by hand in code, even though the file header says no figure is typed by hand. It should come from the top TAX_BRACKETS rate + MEDICARE_LEVY.rate. The sentence also uses LUXURY_CAR_TAX.financialYear as the income year label.

claim: an earlier agent date if the latest return had a tax liability of $20,000 or more, or if a prior-year return was outstanding at 30 June 2026
why: The $20,000 limit and the 30 June 2026 date are typed into the prose. The other dates come from RETURN_2026 (R.*), so these two can drift out of step with them. They belong in RETURN_2026 alongside agentDueDateLargeLiability.

claim: The fund pays the contributions tax on concessional contributions, plus Division 293 tax if your income plus concessional contributions exceeds the threshold.
why: Division 293 is assessed to the individual by the ATO, not withheld by the fund. The individual can choose to pay it from super through a release authority. The page's own Division 293 FAQ (line 71) says you can pay it from your fund or from personal funds.

claim: MLS is "1% to 1.5%" (also "(1% to 1.5%)" at line 244), typed as literals in the prose.
why: The figures are not read from MEDICARE_LEVY.surcharge tier rates, even though the tier list just below renders them from code. If the tiers change, the two could disagree.

claim: Super = 12% of annual earnings (also hard-coded at line 115 '12% SG contribution', and '25%' at lines 23, 50, 61, 62, 70, '38 hours' at lines 29, 39, 81).
why: The values are correct for 2026, but they are typed into JSX instead of coming from SUPER_GUARANTEE.rate / EMPLOYMENT, so they will go stale when the constants change.

claim: In the award's own example, about 90 block hours in a roster period adds roughly $1,656 a month.
why: The unit changes partway through the sentence, from 'a roster period' to 'a month'. The maths works (90 x $18.40 = $1,656), but the period is only right if the award's example roster period is one month. Check against Schedule A.1.7 of the award.

claim: Request additional withholding by lodging a PAYG withholding variation with the ATO, or voluntarily increase your withholding amount with your employer.
why: The ATO's PAYG withholding variation application is used to reduce withholding. You increase withholding by making a written upward-variation agreement with your payer, not by applying to the ATO. Check the wording against the ATO.

claim: Most small businesses do not [pay payroll tax] ... A business with 8 employees averaging $100,000 each ($800,000 total wages) pays zero payroll tax in every state and territory.
why: 'Most small businesses' is a population claim with no source. The $800,000 example is typed rather than checked against MIN_THRESHOLD_STATE. It holds today (the lowest threshold is $1,000,000, and the total with 12% super is $896,000), but it leaves out that super counts as taxable wages, and it would go stale if a threshold fell.

claim: Qualifying earnings are '(for most people, ordinary time earnings)'.
why: Population claim with no figure or source. Qualifying earnings is OTE plus salary-sacrificed amounts; the 'most people' qualifier is unsourced.

claim: lifts the point at which a typical worker starts paying net tax to almost $19,985, or up to $24,985
why: At the 2027-28 rate of 14%, $18,200 + $250/0.14 = $19,985.71 and $18,200 + $950/0.14 = $24,985.71. That is just over the stated figures, so 'almost' looks inverted. Check against Treasury's wording.

claim: The $20,802 grossed-up amount (Type 1) also appears on the employee's income statement as reportable fringe benefits.
why: This is the same error: the RFBA uses the Type 2 gross-up, so on a $10,000 taxable value it is $18,868. The FBT payable figure ($9,777, Type 1) is correct.

claim: Services Australia's DSP page shows the couple Pension Supplement as $65.50 each.
why: This is a typed figure about a third-party page discrepancy and is not held in a constant. It needs re-checking at each 20 March and 20 September indexation, or removing once Services Australia corrects its page.

claim: Returns lodged between July and October 2026 cover FY2025-26, which used the old 16% rate — income tax on $80,000 was ...; the deductions most people forget to claim
why: This is time-bound copy that goes stale after 31 Oct 2026 (agent-lodged returns run later). The locked segment contains an em dash I could not change. 'Most people forget' is a population claim with no source.

claim: The year's settings are now confirmed.
why: The Medicare section on the same page (line 147) says no 2026-27 Medicare levy low-income thresholds have been legislated yet, and the Payday Super cap relief is still pending. 'Settings are now confirmed' overstates it.

claim: Claim the tax-free threshold at your main job only (usually the highest-paying one).
why: 'usually' is an unsourced hedge on a tax rule. The ATO says to claim the threshold from the payer who usually pays the highest salary or wage. Consider wording that follows the ATO's instead of a population hedge.

claim: Every $1,000 in deductions at the 37% marginal rate reduces tax by $370.
why: Both figures are hard-coded. The example also leaves out the Medicare levy, while the Strategy 1 and Strategy 2 figures on the same page include it ($390 on that basis), so the three strategies are worked out on different bases.

claim: reduces by 5 cents for each dollar ... then by 1.5 cents per dollar
why: The cents-per-dollar rates are typed in by hand, but the dollar figures come from LITO.phaseOut1.rate and similar constants. The values are correct for current LITO but could drift.

claim: First-year FAQ answer says 'the $67.15 industry allowance' as a typed literal.
why: The value matches today, but it is hard-coded in prose while the page body and calculator read INDUSTRY_ALLOWANCE.general. It will go stale at the next 1 July update if only the constant changes.

claim: The Annual Wage Review 2026 "lifted award rates and the National Minimum Wage by ${pct(AWR)}" (renders 4.75%).
why: The National Minimum Wage rose 5.97% in the 2026 Annual Wage Review. Only modern award minimums rose 4.75%. The sentence gives the NMW the award figure.

claim: Staff at Licensed Post Offices ... are usually paid under the General Retail Industry Award (also FAQ line 112: 'usually under the Retail Award')
why: This is a population claim with no figure, and the page cites no source for it. It is listed under the pilot lesson on population claims.

claim: New South Wales, Western Australia and the ACT keep the Sunday and add Monday 26 April [2027 Anzac Day].
why: As I recall, NSW law has no substitute day when Anzac Day falls on a weekend (no Monday holiday was added in 2021, for example). The Queensland and NT treatment should also be checked against the FWO 2027 list. I did not verify this.

claim: Leave is worth approximately 14.6% of annual earnings, so the 25% casual loading only provides a ~10% premium over permanent employment.
why: Subtracting percentages on different bases gives the wrong answer. A permanent employee is paid for 260 days but works about 222, so the casual premium is 1.25 / (260/222) - 1, about 6.7%, not ~10%. The FAQ on the same page (employment-type-calculator-faqs.ts line 19, LEAVE_VALUE) uses the worked-days basis and shows about 17%, which contradicts the 14.6% here. The page states two different leave

claim: Personal concessional contributions are taxed at only 15% in the fund.
why: Division 293 tax raises this to 30% when income plus concessional contributions exceed $250,000. The claim is incomplete rather than wrong.

claim: If you receive a taxable payment such as JobSeeker, Youth Allowance or Austudy, you are likely already claiming the threshold from that payment.
why: This is a population hedge with no source. It should state the ATO rule for Centrelink payees (whether the threshold is claimed from the payment) without 'likely'. I left it because changing it would mean stating a rule the page does not cite.

claim: 'Yes, for most people... That's still a {TOP_RATE - COMBINED} tax saving on each dollar contributed'
why: The saving uses the top marginal rate (47%), but Division 293 can apply to someone on the 37% bracket. For that person the saving is smaller (39% vs 30%). 'For most people' is also an unsourced population claim.

claim: Camping allowance $32.19 per working day, maximum $225.36 a week (cl 23.5)
why: Seven days at $32.19 is $225.33, not $225.36. The weekly cap may be a separately rounded award figure, but it is worth a check against Schedule E.

claim: so all weekend work is overtime (cl 29.12, 30.1)
why: The clause cited here (cl 29.12) does not match the clauses used for the same rule in the same file: the header comment (lines 29-31) and BUILDING_OVERTIME (line 92) cite cl 29.4 and 30.1. Check which clause number is right.

claim: Pricing contractor rates ... ignores the 30–40% loading ... A $40/hr employee rate requires approximately $56–$64/hr as a contractor.
why: A 30-40% loading on $40/hr gives $52-$56/hr. $56-$64/hr is a 40-60% loading. Both ranges are hand-typed, and neither comes from contractorRateToEquivalentSalary(), which already drives the rate-to-salary table on the same page.

claim: the zone tax offset, which every NT resident can claim
why: This contradicted the page's own residency test (more than half the income year in the zone, line 103 and the NT FAQ). FIFO workers are also excluded from the offset. I rewrote it as 'which NT residents claim in their tax return'. A reviewer should confirm that wording is acceptable.

claim: Schedule 2 (no TFN)
why: The schedules table on the same page (line 294-295) says Schedule 2 (NAT 1013) covers horticulture and shearing workers, and the no-TFN rates sit inside Schedule 1 (line 291). The ordered list contradicts the table.

claim: Every amount in the standard columns has the 2% Medicare levy built in, including the low-income shading that phases it in rather than applying it from the first dollar.
why: The 'standard columns' include the no-tax-free-threshold column (Scale 1). The low-income Medicare levy phase-in is normally a feature of the threshold-claimed scale (Scale 2), so 'every amount ... including the low-income shading' may be too broad for Scale 1. Please check this against the SCALE_1_NO_TFT coefficients.

claim: WA is the most generous state at the exit (pro-rata payment after 7 years, including on resignation)
why: Victoria's Long Service Leave Act 2018 also pays pro rata after 7 years on any termination, and it lets the leave be taken from 7 years. The ACT pays pro rata from 5 years in some cases. The 'most generous' comparison looks wrong.

claim: BAS lodgement deadlines fall on the 28th of the month following each quarter: 28 October, 28 February, 28 April, and 28 July.
why: The October to December quarter is due 28 February, not the 28th of the month after the quarter (28 January). The rule as worded contradicts the list that follows it.

claim: If your combined earnings exceed ${WHM_CAP}, you may have a tax shortfall because each employer applies the ${WHM_RATE} rate without knowing about the other.
why: Once combined WHM income is above the cap, each employer still withholds 15% on its own share, but the income above the cap is taxed at 30%. So a shortfall is certain, not possible. The existing 'may' softens a definite rule. This line was not changed in this pass; whether to make it definitive is an owner decision.

claim: Tax saved assumes taxable income between $45,001 and $135,000
why: This is correct for 2025-26, but it is hard-coded while the rate next to it comes from THIS.brackets[2]. It will go stale if the brackets change. The same applies to '$18,200' (line 276), 'Employer super at 12%' (line 307) and '1% to 1.5%' MLS (line 277).

claim: Not-for-profit organisations, public hospitals, and charities receive capped FBT exemptions.
why: The claim is too broad. Only PBIs, health promotion charities, public and NFP hospitals and public ambulance services get capped exemptions. Other NFPs and charities are rebatable employers (a rebate, not an exemption), which the same paragraph says later.

claim: A minor benefit is one with a notional taxable value of less than $300.
why: The value is correct, but it is hard-coded in the FAQ and not read from the FBT constants, so it can go stale.

claim: Use your existing fund, or switch to the employer's default if it has lower fees.
why: The answer leaves out super stapling (in force since 1 November 2021). If a new employee makes no choice, the employer must ask the ATO for the employee's stapled fund before it can use its default fund. So the either/or framing is incomplete.

claim: Circumstances it would likely accept include severe illness of you, a carer or your agent
why: The page body (late-tax-return-penalty.tsx line 141) gives the ATO example as 'a registered agent or a person you care for with a severe illness'. 'A carer' (someone who cares for you) and 'a person you care for' are different people, and the body does not mention your own illness. One of the two is wrong. Check against the ATO remission of penalties page.

claim: ...where the Hospitality Industry (General) Award pays 85%. (Line 256 also types 60% for a 17-year-old.)
why: Both figures are correct against the constants (the hospitality age 19 band is 0.85, the retail age 17 band is 0.6). But they are typed into the prose, not taken from HOSPITALITY junior scale / RETAIL_JUNIOR_SCALE. If an AWR or the junior phase-in changes a band, the prose will go stale without anyone noticing.

claim: From 1 July 2026 the superannuation guarantee must be paid with each pay run under Payday Super
why: Payday Super requires contributions to reach the fund within a set number of days after payday. 'Paid with each pay run' simplifies that rule, so check it against the ATO wording. The same claim appears in the FAQ at line 132.

claim: Concessional contributions, including salary sacrifice, are taxed at 15% inside the fund
why: The 15% contributions tax is a typed literal on a page whose header says nothing is typed. It also matches the new FY2026-27 second bracket rate (15%), which makes it easy to confuse with RATE_2 if the bracket changes again.

claim: From 1 July 2027 a driver (thereafter) moves to $1,935.80 a week, or $2,038.00 with the industry allowance.
why: $1,959.60 x 1.04 = $2,037.98 (and $1,935.80 + $98.25 x 1.04 = $2,037.98), so $2,038.00 is 2c off. It may be the figure printed in Schedule 4A, or a rounding slip. Please confirm against the agreement.

claim: This exemption saves a non-resident earning $100,000 a total of $2,000 per year compared to a resident without private health insurance.
why: The 2% Medicare levy is payable whether or not a resident has private health insurance (insurance only affects the surcharge), so that qualifier is misleading. The $2,000 is also hard-coded rather than calculateMedicareLevy(100_000).

claim: A worker who satisfies 4 or more of these indicators as a contractor is more likely to be genuinely independent.
why: No source gives a 4-of-6 threshold. The ATO says no single factor decides status and the whole relationship is weighed. The same section says this two paragraphs earlier, so the line contradicts the page.

claim: Rates run from 4% (Tasmania's first band) to 8.75% (ACT, above $150 million)
why: SA's variable rate phases in from 0% to 4.95% between $1.5m and $1.7m of Australian wages (lib/constants/payroll-tax.ts lines 139-143, and the SA HOW_NOTE on the state page), so 4% is not the lowest rate any employer pays. Either say 'general rates' or name the SA phase-in, as the hub's direct answer does.

claim: The return on voluntary HECS repayments equals the indexation rate avoided (typically 3 to 4% under the CPI/WPI cap). The same 3 to 4% range is repeated at lines 95 and 106.
why: The page's own constant puts the 1 June 2026 rate at 2.8%, which is below this range. With the cap in place, 3 to 4% looks stale as a 'typical' rate.

claim: Leave loading ... is subject to PAYG withholding at the employee's marginal tax rate.
why: PAYG withholding uses the ATO withholding schedules and tax tables, not the employee's marginal rate. The tax is worked out at marginal rates on assessment. The same string also holds an em dash ('would have worked — the ATO treats'), and the checker locks that string as a dash key, so this pass cannot remove it.

claim: the next change is on 20 March 2027
why: This date is typed into the prose. It goes stale after the 20 March 2027 indexation unless someone edits it by hand. RA.indexedOn and RA.ratesFrom already live in constants, so this date should too.

claim: reducing $3 a fortnight per $1,000 above that
why: The figure is correct, but it is typed into the text instead of read from PENSION_ASSETS_TEST.taperPerThousand.single, which the assets-test FAQ on line 34 uses. If the constant changes, this answer will drift.

claim: Businesses with GST turnover of $20 million or more must lodge BAS monthly; STP finalisation 14 July; closely held payees 30 September for employers with 20 or more employees.
why: These thresholds and dates are typed into the prose instead of coming from a constant. They look correct, but nothing ties them to a source.

claim: (3) structuring the business to remain below the state payroll tax threshold, (4) using a mix of casual and part-time workers to minimise leave liability
why: Payroll tax grouping provisions and anti-avoidance rules apply to structuring done to stay under the threshold, so this is risky YMYL advice as worded. Part-time employees accrue leave pro rata, so they do not reduce leave liability per hour worked.

The file header says every figure is interpolated from lib/constants/modern-awards-oct.ts, but these are hard-coded. They match the constants today (CONSTRUCTION_INDUSTRY_ALLOWANCE 67.15, ELECTRICAL_INDUSTRY 41.41) but will drift at the next annual wage review unless they are interpolated.

claim: an administrative uplift of up to 60% that falls to nil on voluntary disclosure within 30 days
why: In SUPER_GUARANTEE_CHARGE.current.upliftSchedule, the uplift is 0 for disclosure within 30 days only when the ATO has made no assessment in the past 2 years. Otherwise it is 20%. The sentence also lists 3 SGC components, but the constant has 4 (choice loading is missing).

claim: The SG does not apply to overtime under the ATO's definition of Ordinary Time Earnings (OTE).
why: Under Payday Super (from 1 July 2026), SG is worked out on qualifying earnings. The sibling novated lease FAQ already uses that term. Overtime is still excluded, but the OTE-only wording may be stale and should be checked against QUALIFYING_EARNINGS.

claim: Casual employees receive a 25% loading on their base hourly rate under the Fair Work Act
why: The 25% casual loading is set by modern awards (and agreements), not directly by the Fair Work Act. The FAQ file builds it from EMPLOYMENT.casualLoading, but this text hard-codes 25% and names the Act as the source.

claim: If you owe $200,000 or less, you may be able to set up a payment plan in ATO online services.
why: The ATO self-serve payment plan limit is typed as a literal.

claim: See what lands in your account after income tax, Medicare and super.
why: The employer pays super guarantee on top of wages, and it is not deducted from take-home pay. Listing super as a deduction from the weekly rate reads as wrong unless the calculator models salary sacrifice.

claim: less beneficial for employees earning under $45,000, those within 2 years of retirement ... most leasing providers offer portability and payout options
why: Editorial judgement stated as fact under a heading about eligibility. The FAQ says there is no legislated income minimum. The 2-year retirement figure and the 'most providers' claim have no source. AUDIT is factual-structured, so this cannot be labelled as opinion in this pass.

claim: Employees who drive more than 15,000 km a year for business typically pay less FBT under the operating cost method.
why: The 15,000 km figure has no source or constant (the statutory rate has been a flat 20% since 2011, whatever the distance). The page cites no source for the population claim, and the employer pays FBT, not the employee.

claim: Most new roles include a 3-6 month probationary period with reduced notice requirements.
why: This is a population claim ('Most new roles') with no cited source. The National Employment Standards notice minimums also do not stop applying during probation. Only the contract or the unfair dismissal minimum employment period differs.

claim: The ATO issues PAYG instalment notices to contractors once they lodge their first tax return showing business income. Instalments are due quarterly.
why: The ATO enrols people in PAYG instalments only when their instalment income and tax payable pass set thresholds, and some people pay annually. 'Once they lodge their first tax return' overstates this.

claim: Seven years of full-time service is the fastest realistic path: one year at Step 1, one year at Step 2 plus confirmation of Proficient accreditation, then one year on each of Steps 3 to 6.
why: The path the FAQ lists adds up to six years (1 + 1 + 4), after which the teacher is on Step 7. 'Seven years' only works if it means 'in your seventh year'. The answer should say either 'six years' or 'you reach Step 7 at the start of your seventh year'. I did not change it.

claim: Resident rates from 1 July 2026
why: The date '1 July 2026' is a typed literal in JSX and does not come from the withholding-schedule constant. It will go stale when the rates roll over.

claim: Aides, assistants and directors who are not university-qualified ECTs: "most of them are covered by the Children's Services Award 2010"
why: This is a claim about how many people it covers, with no figure and no cited source. The award text excludes them (cl 4.4(c)) but does not say how many fall under MA000120. Either cite FWO coverage guidance or cut it back to 'are generally covered by the Children's Services Award 2010 [MA000120]', which is an editorial call.

claim: a bricklayer's minimum is ${money2(toCents(41.22 - tool))} a week below a carpenter's on the same site
why: The carpenter tool allowance is typed in as 41.22 instead of using the CARPENTER_TOOL_ALLOWANCE constant. When the allowance changes on 1 July, this gap will drift away from the carpenter page. The comparison also holds only for the CW3 bricklayer, not for the CW5 refractory bricklayer.

claim: There is no partial or pro-rata discount for holding an asset for eleven months.
why: 'eleven months' is a typed literal. It is tied to CGT_MINIMUM_OWNERSHIP_MONTHS - 1 and goes stale if that constant changes. The question text and the other answers interpolate the constant.

claim: A boilermaker employed on a building site by a builder or contractor ... may be under a different award
why: The coverage text hedges ('may be under a different award'), but the workforce section at line 83 says it definitively: the Building and Construction General On-site Award applies to a boilermaker on a building site. The two statements should use the same modality.

claim: Their hourly rate normally includes a 25% casual loading
why: 'Normally' hedges a figure that line 355 states as a rule for minimum-wage casuals. The 25% is also typed by hand and not taken from a casual-loading constant, so the two lines can drift apart.

claim: Employees in the 15% bracket 'are better served by claiming the Low Income Tax Offset instead'.
why: LITO is applied automatically at assessment, so nobody claims it. It is also not an alternative to salary sacrifice. As written, the advice is misleading.

claim: a 1.5% workers compensation premium
why: This is hard-coded in the prose while the table uses TABLE_WORKCOVER (currently 0.015). The two agree today but will drift if the constant changes.

claim: The zone tax offset itself is not assessable income for Centrelink purposes, so claiming it does not affect your payments.
why: A tax offset reduces tax payable. It is not a payment received, so calling it 'not assessable income for Centrelink purposes' looks like a mix-up with the ATO rule that the Centrelink/DVA remote area allowance is not taxable. Confirm the source and what the sentence should say.

claim: About to cross a repayment threshold: if your income is close to a higher HECS repayment band, paying down the debt before 1 June can reduce the indexation amount applied that year.
why: The condition (income near a higher repayment band) has nothing to do with the effect (lower indexation). Under the marginal system the compulsory repayment depends on repayment income, not on the balance. This bullet looks like a muddled merge of two separate points.

claim: The pay rise at the end of an adult painting apprenticeship is small: $28.59 a week in the wage part before allowances, by our arithmetic.
why: The adult rate of $1,090.54 includes the $9.89 tool allowance and the $67.15 industry allowance, so its wage part is $1,013.50 (the residential $1,077.11 less $53.72 and $9.89 gives the same). That is $105.60 below the $1,119.10 standard rate, not $28.59. Even comparing the full $1,090.54 with $1,119.10 gives $28.56. The 'close to the standard rate' framing in the same sentence depends on this fig

claim: Same result as the ATO look-up table: cents are ignored and the Schedule 1 formula is applied exactly.
why: The widget renders on the monthly pages too. For monthly pay the ATO says to enter earnings including cents (with the 33-cent rule), as monthly-tax-table-faqs.ts line 40 and monthly-tax-table.tsx line 176 say. So 'cents are ignored' is wrong for the monthly cycle. The note text should depend on the frequency.

claim: This calculator provides estimates based on current ATO PAYG withholding schedules.
why: Job 1 and the combined figures are not withholding. They are year-end liability from calculateIncomeTax minus LITO plus calculateMedicareLevy. Only Job 2 uses the Schedule 1 withholding scale. I fixed the Job 2 sentence, which still said 'approximate rate' after the code moved to the real scale. The first sentence of this legal notice was left alone.

claim: Under most awards Saturday work pays around {saturdayMin} to {saturdayMax} of the base rate ... penalty rates apply ... typically weekends, public holidays, overtime and late nights.
why: This is a population claim ('most awards') and the page cites no source for it. The ranges come from EMPLOYMENT.penaltyRates, but the 'most awards' coverage cannot be checked.

claim: the ATO refunds the excess when you lodge your tax return in July or August.
why: Self-lodgers can lodge until 31 October, and later through a tax agent. 'July or August' reads as the only lodgement window.

claim: No Medicare levy exemption (bullet heading in the list of benefits non-residents lose)
why: Non-residents ARE exempt from the levy. The bullet body actually describes losing access to Medicare services. The bold heading (locked) is misleading and should be something like 'No Medicare access'.

claim: You need a record of the actual hours you worked from home for the whole year.
why: The answer is incomplete. The ATO's fixed-rate method also needs a document (such as a bill) for each type of running expense the rate covers. Nothing was added, because adding it would be a new fact.

claim: 'At a 6% mortgage rate, salary sacrifice into super typically delivers a better after-tax outcome because the concessional tax rate is lower than the marginal rate'
why: The 6% is hardcoded and has no source. The argument compares a tax-rate gap with a mortgage rate but does not account for the expected super return. It is an opinion presented as a rule, so it needs labelled editorial judgment or a worked figure from code.

claim: Everywhere except the ACT (completed years and months) the part year counts down to the day.
why: The methodology bullet (line 550) and the spoke basis text (line 642) both say Queensland uses its own years/months/weeks/days table, so 'down to the day' does not quite match Queensland.

claim: Agent clients whose latest return had a tax liability of $20,000 or more are due 31 March 2027.
why: $20,000 is typed into the prose here and again in the TAX_CALENDAR_2026_27 event title. It is not taken from a constant, so the two copies can drift apart.

claim: Field label "Your age at 30 June 2027" and hint "Turning 60 by 30 June 2027 means the lower tax rate."
why: The year is typed into the code. It matches REDUNDANCY_TAX.incomeYear 2026-27 today but goes stale when the income year rolls over, while the intro text (line 46) uses the constant.

claim: Centrelink use of adjusted taxable income (which includes reportable super contributions) is 'potentially reducing eligibility for Family Tax Benefit, childcare subsidies'.
why: Adjusted taxable income adds the sacrificed amount back, so it stays roughly the same with or without the sacrifice. The risk is that the sacrifice does not raise benefit eligibility. It does not reduce it. The wording is hedged ('may', 'potentially') and the program name should be 'Child Care Subsidy'. Needs a factual rewrite against Services Australia guidance.

claim: keeping the 30% marginal rate for incomes between $45,001 and $135,000 ... the FY2024-25 / FY2025-26 comparison table (tax-free threshold, brackets, 11.5%/12% SG, 2% Medicare levy)
why: The bracket boundaries and rates in this paragraph and the table are hard-coded, while the rest of the page reads them from TAX_BRACKETS_2025_26 and MEDICARE_LEVY. They are correct for 2025-26 but will drift if the constants change.

claim: Current rates are column C (from 15 November 2025); next rise around mid-November 2026; Extra Cheque next paid 19 November 2026
why: These are not wrong, but they go stale in about three weeks (today is 27 Oct 2026). Column D and the Extra Cheque date need updating soon after 15 to 19 November 2026.

claim: HECS-HELP repayments for employees with a study debt above {HECS_HELP.minimumThreshold}
why: The HELP threshold applies to repayment income, not to the size of the study debt. Line 333 states the rule correctly.

page: https://pay-calculator-australia.com/public-holiday-pay/ (award rates table) and the restaurant and clerks award calculator notes
claim: Restaurant note cites cl 24.4(d), and the Clerks note on line 84 cites the same cl 24.4(d)
why: Two different awards share an identical clause reference. One of them may be a copy-paste error, so check each against its own award text.

claim: A $2,000 deduction at the 30% marginal rate reduces your tax by $600 (also table line 351: $600)
why: Both the rate and the saving are typed into the copy, not taken from B2.rate. The figure also leaves out the 2% Medicare levy saving (a $2,000 deduction saves $640 including Medicare). Line 309 types '30% marginal rate' and '80_000 * 0.3' in the same way.

claim: Medicare levy written as a literal '2%' at lines 79, 193 and 228, plus 'applies to most Australian residents' at line 79
why: The figure is correct today (MEDICARE_LEVY.rate = 0.02), but it is typed into the copy while the lead paragraph uses MEDICARE_PCT, so it will not change if the constant does. 'Most Australian residents' is a population claim with no source.

claim: FAQ: 'no child can work between 10pm and 6am' (any child). The youngWorkers paragraph at line 453 puts the same 10pm to 6am limit under 'a school-aged child'.
why: The two passages give the 10pm to 6am night limit different scopes on the same page (all children or school-aged children only). The Child Employment Act 2006 / QLD_CHILD_RULES source should settle which is right.

claim: Service outside the ACT may not count.
why: This states a rule with a hedge. Check WorkSafe ACT Guidance Note 067 for the exact condition under which service outside the ACT is excluded, then state it definitively. I left the wording as it was because I could not verify the rule.

claim: Administrative uplift of up to 60% that falls to nil on a voluntary disclosure within 30 days
why: The 30-day voluntary-disclosure condition for a nil uplift under the Payday Super SGC needs checking against the final legislation or ATO guidance. It is a hard-coded figure with no constant.

claim: 'unused cap from the last five years' and FAQ line 36 'each expires after five years' use the literal word 'five'
why: The rule is correct today, but 'five' is not tied to CARRY_FORWARD.years, which the same text uses elsewhere through an expression. The two will drift if the constant changes.

claim: On your TFN Declaration, tick "Yes" if you have a HELP, VSL, SFSS, or TSL debt.
why: The current ATO TFN declaration lists HELP, VSL, FS (Financial Supplement), SSL (Student Start-up Loan) and TSL. 'SFSS' is the old name, and SSL is missing from the list.

claim: Engineering technicians and draftspersons "are usually covered by the Manufacturing Award or an industry award instead"
why: A hedged coverage statement with no clause cited. The page gives clause numbers for every other coverage rule.

claim: Since 1 July 2022, all employees receive super regardless of monthly earnings.
why: 'All employees' is too broad. Employees under 18 still get SG only if they work more than 30 hours in a week.

claim: the law as passed uses realised earnings that each super fund calculates and reports to the ATO
why: The page states that the revised Division 296 law has passed. Check its passage and start date against the ATO 'Better targeted superannuation concessions' page this article cites, because the reviewer could not confirm the bill's status.

claim: 13 weeks starting Monday 1 August ends Monday 31 October.
why: 13 weeks is 91 days. Counted from Monday 1 August, the 91st day of leave is Sunday 30 October, and Monday 31 October is the day the employee returns to work. Check SafeWork SA's exact wording (it probably says 'returns on Monday 31 October') and say 'ends Sunday 30 October' or 'returns to work Monday 31 October'.

claim: Contributions are taxed at 15% in the fund, compared to your marginal rate (which could be 30-45%).
why: Hard-coded rates. The phrase "could be 30-45%" leaves out the 16% bracket and the Division 293 extra 15% for high incomes. Both should come from lib/constants tax brackets and the contributions tax rate.

claim: The Clerk Grade 9/10 FAQ dates the rates 'From 1 July 2026', while the 5/6 FAQ and the schedule say 'the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026'.
why: The effective date is worded two ways on one page, and the Crown award's operative date is the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026. Wording consistency should be checked against the source (not changed in this pass).

claim: Australian employees are entitled to 7 distinct types of leave
why: The 7-row table counts annual leave twice (standard and shift workers) and leaves out NES family and domestic violence leave (10 days paid). The count does not match the NES list.

claim: Claiming the tax-free threshold reduces your weekly withholding by approximately $67
why: The figure is typed in and the gap between the two scales changes with income and financial year. It should be worked out with withholdingForPeriod(gross, 'weekly', 'noTft') minus withholdingForPeriod(gross, 'weekly', 'tft') at a stated gross.

claim: separate from the 6% national minimum wage increase (also line 38: "rose 6% to $26.44 an hour")
why: $24.95 to $26.44 is +5.97%, which is the figure the brief lists as correct. 6% is a rounded, hard-coded figure, not a value derived from code. lib/news.ts line 70 also says 6%.

claim: overtime is paid at penalty rates of 1.5x or 2x
why: Awards treat overtime rates and penalty rates as separate terms. The multipliers also vary by award, so this reads as a universal rule.

claim: 14 July 2026: Employers must finalise Single Touch Payroll data
why: The date is hard-coded here and again at line 286 ('due by 14 July'), while every other deadline in the table comes from RETURN_2026. It is correct for this return but will go stale.

claim: a gig worker earning $80,000 in the 30% bracket who contributes $10,000 to super saves $1,500 in tax (30% marginal rate minus 15% super tax = 15% x $10,000)
why: The worked example ignores the 2% Medicare levy, which a deductible contribution also reduces. That makes the saving about $1,700, not $1,500. All of these figures are hard-coded.

claim: Your figures will differ if you have a study loan, salary sacrifice arrangements or additional income.
why: This contradicts the HECS section at line 111, which says the take-home figures apply whether or not you carry a HECS-HELP debt, because $52,254.80 is below the $69,528 threshold. A study loan changes the figures only when combined with other income.

claim: When you salary package benefits (other than super), your employer reports the grossed-up taxable value as a Reportable Fringe Benefits Amount (RFBA).
why: RFBA is reported only when an employee's total taxable value of reportable benefits is over $2,000 in the FBT year (FBT.reportableThreshold). Exempt items such as portable electronic devices (the s58X work-related items) are not reportable at all, so 'any benefit other than super' claims too much.

claim: Common reasons for a withholding variation include ... salary sacrifice arrangements that reduce assessable income; example '$5,000+ in tools or uniforms'
why: Salary sacrifice already lowers taxable gross through payroll and does not need a section 15-15 variation. The $5,000 example has no source.

claim: Concessional and non-concessional caps are indexed periodically in line with wage growth, via increments to the general transfer balance cap. ... the general transfer balance cap moving from $2.0 million to $2.1 million, which flows through to lift both contribution caps (line 53)
why: The concessional cap is indexed to AWOTE in $2,500 steps and the non-concessional cap is set at 4x the concessional cap. why: Since the Closing Loopholes amendments (2024), the s357 Fair Work Act defence is that the employer 'reasonably believed' the contract was one for services. The page's wording roughly inverts that test, so check it against the current s357.

claim: Non-residents can claim a 'Foreign Income Tax Offset' (FITO) in their home country for Australian tax paid, or claim an offset in Australia for tax paid overseas
why: FITO is Australia's own offset; a home country gives its own foreign tax credit. Also, non-residents are not taxed in Australia on foreign income, so they generally have no Australian FITO claim.

claim: A $2,000 laptop packaged at the 30% marginal rate saves $600 in income tax.

claim: Workers compensation insurance costs contractors $500-$3,000 annually depending on industry and risk classification.

If a worker's income is above the WHM cap, the WHM rate there is already 30%, so withholding does not double across the whole year. The sentence is accurate as a comparison of the two rates. The owner may want 'on income up to the WHM cap' added, which only a structure or fact pass can do.

claim: The 2/1 roster maximises earning potential (about 243 days a year), but the highest-paying rosters are those with longer swings (3/1 or 4/1).
why: The answer contradicts itself. A 3/1 or 4/1 roster works a larger share of the year than 2/1, so 2/1 cannot be the roster that maximises earnings. The 243 days figure is also hard-coded rather than derived.

claim: In the NT, you are entitled to 13 weeks of long service leave after 10 years of continuous service
why: The wording matches the entitlement in the Long Service Leave Act 1981 (NT), and the writer's removal of 'may be eligible' is correct. But the answer feeds FAQPage schema and reads on its own, and its 'you' covers groups the Act does not: NT Government and Australian Government employees and NT Build construction workers, who the page body excludes at source line ~166. The owner should confirm the

claim: Most Australian midwives work in state public hospitals, and they are not paid under this award.

why: The arithmetic does not match. 27,040 ÷ 521.7 is about 51.83, not 52. 27,040 ÷ 520 is exactly 52, and 52 × 8.667 = 450.684, so either the divisor should be 520 weeks or the hours total is wrong. Check it against the Wageline 'Payment of long service leave' page (WA_PAY).

claim: $147,590 for advice and assessment specialists is typed into the FAQ answer.
why: The value matches the data today, but it is hard-coded while the other three medians in the same sentence come from CYBER_SECURITY_ATO.rows. A future data update would leave it stale. It should read from ROWS[2].medianSalary.

claim: Superannuation ... 12% ... $60.00 (example 20 hrs @ $25/hr)

claim: Two strategies legally reduce your taxable income and increase your after-tax pay: salary sacrifice and work-related deductions.
why: Salary sacrifice lowers the amount paid to your bank account. The page's own strategy table (line 346) says 'Increases Bank Deposit? No (funds go to super)'. It saves tax overall but does not increase after-tax pay. The section also has a third strategy (private health insurance), but that one does not reduce taxable income, so the count of two is defensible.

claim: If a business hires you primarily for your labour ... they may be required to pay the SG super guarantee on your behalf.

I did not change the modality.

claim: Frequent commission payments can trigger PAYG instalment obligations if your total income exceeds ATO thresholds.
why: PAYG instalments apply to business and investment income. An employee's commission is covered by PAYG withholding (Schedule 5), not instalments, so the sentence looks wrong for employees. It is also vague: it names no threshold.

claim: this is the first full year the marginal repayment system and the FY2026-27 threshold settings interact with an assessment, after 2.8% indexation was applied on 1 June 2026
why: Tax time 2026 assesses 2025-26 income, so the 2025-26 HELP repayment thresholds apply, not FY2026-27 settings. The marginal repayment system started 1 July 2025, so this is the first year it is assessed at all, not the 'first full year'. Please also confirm the 2.8% 1 June 2026 indexation figure.

claim: The ATO's own example: contracts exchanged on 4 June 2026 and settlement on 6 July 2026, gain belongs in the return for the year ending 30 June 2026.
why: This is presented as the ATO's own example, but the dates are typed literals. The ATO's published example may use different years, so a re-dated example would be a misquote. Check it against ATO QC104071 / QC69844, or drop the 'ATO's own example' attribution if the dates were changed by the site.

claim: it reflects the many people paid under enterprise agreements and with overtime

why: The weekly page has two 'Download CSV' buttons. TableDownloads (table-downloads.tsx:51, using downloads-manifest.json) serves a fixed 2026-27 file covering $1 to $3,400 (3,400 rows). FullTaxTable (full-tax-table.tsx:74) builds the file in the browser up to CSV_TABLE_RANGES.weekly.to ($5,000) for the selected year. The FAQ only describes the second button, so a reader can click the wrong one. The f

claim: someone on 37c in the dollar than to someone on 15c
why: Correct for 2026-27, but the rates are typed into the prose rather than read from TAX_BRACKETS like the FAQ file does. They will go stale on 1 July 2027 when the bottom rate changes.

claim: On {NOW.days} days at the 2026-27 rate ...
why: '2026-27' is hard-coded, but the figure uses RATE = PPL_RATES[PPL_CURRENT_FY]. The label will be wrong when PPL_CURRENT_FY rolls over.

claim: the next change is 20 March 2027
why: The next indexation date is typed by hand next to the PP.indexedOn constant. It will go stale after March 2027.

why: Taper rates (50c, 60c, 40c) are fixed percentages and cannot index. The $150 and $256 allowance thresholds also appear to have stayed the same for several years, so it is not clear they index on 1 July at all. The same claim is in the code comments at line 49 of this file and lines 266 and 537 of the constants file.

claim: far above the award, because most engineers are paid market salaries
why: A population claim with no figure or cited source. The JSA median shows earnings sit above the award, but it does not show that most engineers are on market salaries.

claim: Modern award rates are the legal minimum pay for most Australian employees.
why: This is a population claim with no figure or source. ABS Employee Earnings and Hours puts award-only employees at roughly a quarter of all employees. Awards are only the BOOT reference point for agreement employees, so 'most' needs a source or narrower wording. I left it unchanged because it is the protected first sentence of the direct answer.

claim: Progression in {state} is not simply one step per calendar year.
why: This sentence renders on every state page. The state's own progression data partly contradicts it: NT 'One increment every 12 months, and it is hard to withhold', WA 'An annual increment to 2.9', VIC 'Progression happens once a year, on 1 May'. It holds for NSW (accreditation gate) and SA (207 duty days). For NT it reads as wrong.

why: Only 3 of 8 states have a nextIncrease (nt, tas, vic). act, nsw, qld, sa and wa have nextIncrease: null, so their pages show no next-increase date. The vic value is a pending status, not a date. The string is locked (faqs.push call arg), so I could not narrow it. Suggested wording: '... leadership rates and, where the agreement already sets one, the date of its next increase'.

claim: Commission can lift a HECS-HELP repayment 'into a higher band' (same wording in commission-tax-faqs.ts line 66: 'higher repayment band').
why: From 2025-26, compulsory HELP repayments use a marginal system on income above the threshold, not the old percentage bands. 'Band' may describe the pre-2025 system.

Line 230 (methodology), line 45 (source title 'Company tax rates 2025–26' and URL) and the FAQ in tech-salary-guide-australia-faqs.ts line 67 say the same. The rate is probably unchanged, but the year label and source link look stale. Confirm against the ATO 2026-27 company tax rates

claim: January indexation reflects "movements in the Consumer Price Index over the preceding six months"
why: Youth Allowance, Austudy, ABSTUDY and Carer Allowance are indexed once a year on 1 January, so the measure should be annual CPI (12 months to the September quarter), not six months. Six-monthly CPI is the pension cycle.

claim: lifted the national minimum wage by 6%
why: The exact figure is 5.97% ($24.95 to $26.44). The rounding is consistent across the headline, the title and the key facts '+6%' (line 18). Listed only so a reviewer can decide whether a YMYL page should show the exact figure.

claim: On 3 May 2026 the ACT Government delayed the entry of hairdressing and beauty, and accommodation and food services, into the Services Industry Scheme until 1 January 2027.
why: 3 May 2026 is a Sunday, which is an unusual date for a government decision or notifiable instrument. Check the date against the ACT Leave or ACT Legislation Register notice.

claim: Revised Stage 3: '45% above $190,001' (line 102 also says 'raised the top threshold to $190,001').
why: The 45% rate applies above $190,000 (from $190,001). 'Above $190,001' is off by one dollar.

claim: Leave loading of 17.5% is paid 'under many awards and enterprise agreements'
why: Population claim with no count and no source cited on the page (brief lesson: population claims go to factQuestions).

claim: Four changes from 1 July 2026: Payday Super, the cut to the 15% rate, the indexed HECS-HELP threshold, and the annual maximum super contribution base.
why: The list below this intro (lines 358-361) has Payday Super, the tax cut, the HECS threshold and the Income Statement deadline. It has no maximum contribution base item, so the intro and the list name different fourth changes.

claim: Emergency service workers, healthcare professionals, and essential infrastructure employees face different reasonableness thresholds
why: This is an unsourced claim. s62(3) weighs the nature of the role and the needs of the workplace, but it sets no separate thresholds for named groups.

why: The Work Bonus credit is typed into the hint as $300. Everywhere else it comes from WORK_BONUS.fortnightlyCredit, so this hint will go stale if the constant changes.

why: The Long Service Corporation also runs a portable scheme for the contract cleaning industry. The sentence is incomplete rather than wrong. It needs checking against longservice.nsw.gov.au.

claim: Salary provides income stability, paid leave and predictable budgeting.
why: Permanent hourly employees get the same NES paid leave. Only casuals miss out, so presenting paid leave as a salary advantage over hourly pay is misleading.

claim: The Nurses Award 2020 is the single most searched-for nursing pay document in Australia ... It sets the minimum below which no nurse in the country may lawfully be paid.
why: 'Single most searched-for' has no cited source. 'No nurse in the country' overreaches: the modern award covers national-system employers, and state public sector nurses in the state industrial systems (NSW, Qld, WA, SA, Tas) are covered by state instruments, not the federal award.

why: 1 July 2026 is itself a Wednesday. A Wednesday-to-Tuesday cycle therefore starts the new rate on 1 July, and no July pay period carries days at the old rate. The example needs a different start day (for example Monday). The lib/news.ts FAQ answer uses the same Wednesday example.

claim: The same update lifted the Medicare levy low-income thresholds and re-indexed the study and training loan repayment thresholds across all 15 withholding schedules.
why: No constant backs the hard-coded count of 15 schedules or the claim that all of them were reissued on 1 July 2026. Please check both against the ATO's 2026-27 schedule list.

claim: QPS says back payments began in the pay fortnight of 24 June 2026 with all adjustments expected to be finished by 5 August 2026.
why: This is stale. As of 27 Oct 2026 the 5 August 2026 completion date has passed, but the notice still describes it as a future expectation. Someone needs to confirm with the QPS CPI Uplift Adjustment page that the back payments are finished, then reword it in the past tense or remove it.

claim: Removing LMITO from FY2022-23 raised the tax payable by earners between $37,000 and $126,000 (also line 218: 'up to $1,500 more tax for earners between $37,000 and $126,000').
why: LMITO also paid a base amount ($255, or $675 in FY2021-22) to earners at or below $37,000, so they lost it too. The $1,500 maximum applied only from about $48,001 to $90,000. The range looks too narrow.

why: This figure is typed by hand and does not come from the SUPER_NET or fv code the table uses. Its basis is unstated: whether it is gross or net of the 15% contributions tax, fees and earnings tax. It should be computed with fv() like the table values.

claim: In some cases, the Fair Work Ombudsman or courts may award interest on unpaid wages, particularly for prolonged underpayments.
why: The FWO is a regulator and does not award interest; only a court can order it. This contradicts the page's own FAQ ('Interest is not part of a standard Fair Work claim, but a court can order interest'). The phrase 'particularly for prolonged underpayments' has no source.

why: 'may not' reads as a hedge on a rule. Where the PSI rules apply, the income is attributed to you and taxed at your marginal rates, so the company does not lower the tax. This string was outside the writer's changes and is not edited in this pass. Flagged for a definitive rewrite.

The intro was written as 'partly before tax and partly after tax' so it does not repeat the claim.

claim: 2026-27 is one of those years if you're paid on a Wednesday: see pay periods in 2026-27.

why: Victoria also lets employees take leave after 7 years (STATE_PROFILES.VIC.longServiceLeave.takeAfterYears = 7, line 289, with 6.07 weeks). The ACT ties with Victoria on the qualifying period. Its only clear lead is pro-rata from 5 years, and NSW also starts pro-rata at 5. The ACT page intro (modules/state/pay-calculator-act.tsx:153, 'faster than anywhere else in Australia: 7 years') repeats the cl

claim: Most centres pay more than this award.
why: Population claim with no figure. The page cites only the Worker Retention Payment rules, not how many providers take the grant. The FAQ answer at line 199 ('Often, yes.') makes the same claim.

why: A population claim with no figure and no source cited on the page. It is probably right (ATO guidance), but under the brief it needs a source or a review.

claim: preservation age (${PRESERVATION_AGE} for most Australians)

why: The ATO publishes the Medicare levy and its low-income thresholds, which are set in Treasury legislation. Services Australia runs Medicare enrolment, not the levy thresholds. The source label looks wrong.
