why: This is a hard-coded range with no source or derivation in code. 4 weeks of annual leave plus 10 days of personal leave comes to about 11.5%, so the 15% upper end needs a stated basis.

claim: Income tax card: "progressive rates from 0% to 45%" is hardcoded.
why: The rates should come from TAX_BRACKETS[0].rate and the top bracket rate so the card cannot drift from the bracket table.

claim: An accountant is worth it if gig income exceeds $30,000-$40,000.
why: This is a hard-coded editorial threshold with no source. The page AUDIT does not flag it as labelled editorial judgment.

claim: The fixed rate is 70 cents per hour for FY2024-25 and FY2025-26 (67 cents for FY2022-23 and FY2023-24)
why: The methodology note hard-codes 70 cents, but the rest of the page renders RETURN_2026.wfhFixedRateCents. When the 2026-27 rate is published, this note will drift from the page.

claim: For example, $3,360 of super guarantee gives 15% = $504
why: The 15% is hard-coded, but the sentence before it uses NOW.rate. The figure is correct (it is the ATO example), but it is not tied to the constant.

claim: The fixed rate method suits most employees
why: This is a population or opinion claim with no source, and it is in the first sentence of the answer. The AUDIT marks the page factual-structured, not editorial.

claim: No deposit is required in most novated lease arrangements.
why: Population claim with no source.

claim: (from 1 July 2026) ... Many industries have award rates that are higher than the minimum wage.
why: The date is typed by hand instead of being read from NMW_ORDER.operativeFrom. "Many industries" is a population claim with no source. It also needs checking now that the national minimum wage rose 5.97% while award minimums rose 4.75%.

claim: a public holiday calendar with two part-days and a Brisbane-only show day
why: QLD_HOLIDAYS lists only one part-day holiday for Queensland (Christmas Eve, 6 pm to midnight). Queensland has no New Year's Eve part-day, so 'two part-days' does not match the site's own data. Left unchanged.

claim: four part-day and Proclamation Day holidays that other states do not have
why: The wording was ambiguous. I read it as Christmas Eve part-day + New Year's Eve part-day + Proclamation Day + the 28 December additional day = 4, all flagged stateSpecific in SA_HOLIDAYS, and rewrote it that way. 'That other states do not have' was wrong for Christmas Eve, because Queensland also has a Christmas Eve part-day. Please confirm the 'four' reading.

claim: Notice and FAQ answers type the figures as literals: $33.99/hr, $1,291.80/wk, $67,174/yr, $42.49 casual (line 125) and the NMW $26.44/hr, $1,004.90/wk (lines 112, 129), plus the solicitor median $2,070/wk and $107,640/yr (line 137).
why: They are correct today: they match LAW_GRADUATE, EMPLOYMENT.minimumWageHourly/Weekly and MEDIAN. Because they are typed in the prose rather than built from those constants, they will go stale at the next Annual Wage Review (1 July 2027) unless someone edits them by hand. The landscaper file builds the same kind of figures from expressions.

claim: two $75 instalments from 1 July to 31 December 2025 ... ended on 31 December 2025
why: The end date is typed out even though COST_OF_LIVING_FACTS.energyBillReliefEnded already exists and is used in the first COL FAQ. The two could drift apart. The $75 instalment is also a literal.

claim: Yes, most leasing providers accept used vehicles that are under 7 years old at the end of the proposed lease term.
why: This claims something about most providers and gives a hard age limit, but no source is cited. Provider age limits differ, and several allow older cars at the end of the lease. The mechanical-inspection and clear-title requirements are also unsourced provider policy stated as a rule.

claim: Allowances cited as "Appendix 2 Part 2" (also lines 113 and 230)
why: The file header cites the allowances as Appendix 2A Part 2 (wages are Appendix 2A Part 1). The visible citation may be missing the "A".

claim: Employees with irregular income, multiple jobs, or mid-year start dates frequently receive a refund
why: This is a population claim with no source. People with multiple jobs more often end up with a shortfall, because each payer withholds as if its pay were the only income.

claim: Reversing losses and discount "is the most common error in third-party CGT calculators"
why: This claims something about a whole population of calculators, gives no figure and cites no source. I left it unchanged. Either source it or cut it.

claim: If you started your job after 17 August 1993 (which covers essentially every current employee)
why: This is a population claim with no figure and no source. It is probably true, but under the brief's rule it gets flagged and the text was left unchanged.

claim: WorkCover cost ranges from 0.3% to 8% of payroll depending on the industry and state.
why: Unsourced typed range. Some state and industry premium rates may fall outside it.

claim: NMW_DECISION.citation = "[2026] FWCFB 3500" (also lib/constants/junior-rates.ts:42, schads-award.ts:55, coles.ts:145)
why: The same decision number is used for two years: lib/data/employer-pay/coles.ts:144 cites "[2025] FWCFB 3500" for the 2025 Annual Wage Review. Two reviews a year apart sharing one decision number is unlikely. Check the 2026 citation against the FWC decision.

claim: Most architects are paid a contract salary above these figures
why: This is a population claim with no figure or source in the sentence. The JSA median ($2,308 a week) on the same page supports it only loosely, because a median says nothing about 'most' being paid above the award.

claim: Most Victorian private-sector employees are covered by federal modern awards ... Victorian state public sector staff ... are usually on Victorian agreements instead
why: 'Most' and 'usually' are population claims with no source. Victoria referred its powers in 1996, so all Victorian private-sector employees are in the national system. Victorian public sector agreements are also approved under the Fair Work Act, so calling them 'Victorian agreements' could mislead.

claim: Older payslips may show the same deduction as "HECS", "HELP", or "SFSS"; they all mean the same thing.
why: The Student Financial Supplement Scheme (SFSS) was a separate loan. Before 1 July 2019 its compulsory repayment was a separate withholding component, apart from HELP. An older payslip line labelled SFSS was not the same deduction as HECS/HELP, although all of them are now combined under STSL. The sentence should say that the labels are now combined under STSL, not that they mean the same thing.

claim: Most youth workers sit at Level 2 or Level 3, depending on their qualification and whether they supervise others.
why: This is a claim about how many youth workers sit at each level, with no figure and no cited source. The page's own FAQ also lists Level 4 as a possible level.

claim: 'with most councils paying above it [the Local Government Industry Award] under an enterprise agreement.'
why: This is a population claim with no figure and no cited source, and it renders on all 8 state pages. Either cite a source or soften it to a checkable statement.

claim: The Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS) is an additional tax on top of the standard 2% Medicare levy. (The 2% is also typed in at line 124, and the LHC 2% / 70% / age 40 / 20% figures at lines 206 to 212.)
why: The figures are correct but typed into the prose. The hero uses formatMlsRate(MEDICARE_LEVY.rate) and the FAQ file uses LHC_PER_YEAR / LHC_MAX, so the page and the FAQ can fall out of step.

claim: Employees on Award-free contracts, common in professional services, banking, and technology
why: This is a population claim with no source. Banking is largely covered by the Banking, Finance and Insurance Award 2020, which provides 17.5% annual leave loading. Line 289 ('Award-free employees on individual contracts rarely receive the 17.5% leave loading') is also an unsourced population claim.

claim: Every employer in Australia must hold workers compensation insurance, regardless of business size or number of employees ... Sole traders with no employees are the only exception in most states.
why: Some schemes exempt employers with a very small wage bill (for example, Victoria's rateable remuneration minimum for registration), so 'regardless of business size' looks too absolute. 'In most states' has no source.

claim: Because the value ranges overlap at the top, the last step of one grade can pay more than the first step of the next: VPS 4.1.7 pays $114,476 while VPS 5.1.1 pays $116,413
why: The data has no overlap between grades. Every grade's top step pays less than the next grade's first step, and the example given shows 4.1.7 paying LESS than 5.1.1. The sentence contradicts its own example. Its conclusion (promotion from the top of grade 4 is smaller than one grade 4 step) holds, but 'overlap' and 'can pay more' look wrong.

claim: Typically, no. Most contracts quote base salary with super paid on top of it.
why: This is a population claim ('most contracts') with no figure and no cited source.

claim: training.gov.au released CPC30326 on 23 September 2026 and marked CPC30220 superseded from 22 September 2026.
why: The superseded date comes one day before the replacement's release date. One of the two dates looks transposed. Check against training.gov.au.

claim: 'However, casual employees earn more gross income (due to loading) for the same hours, which may place them in a higher tax bracket.' Also '$70,000/year' is typed into the text.
why: The hedge 'may' and the hard-coded $70,000 example were already there (the writer did not add them). Under marginal rates only the income above a threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so 'higher tax bracket' needs careful wording. The example figure is not held in a constant.

claim: check your income support payment or FTB Part A in its own calculator, listed under Related Calculators and Guides
why: The eligible-payment list includes Carer Payment, Disability Support Pension, ABSTUDY, Farm Household Allowance and Special Benefit. None of these has a calculator in CentrelinkRelated, so readers on those payments have nowhere to check. The original wording had the same gap.

claim: Tax brackets, LITO thresholds, and HECS repayment rates change at the start of each financial year on 1 July.
why: LITO thresholds ($700, $37,500, $66,667) have not changed in years, and brackets do not change every year. Only HECS thresholds are indexed each year. As written, this claims a yearly change that does not happen.

claim: The usual explanation is long service leave: by 10 years most employees also qualify for it ... many agreements keep paying more after 10 years.
why: These are population claims ('most employees', 'many agreements') with no figure and no cited source, and the attribution 'The usual explanation' is vague. The page should either cite the 2004 Redundancy Case reasoning (Fair Work Commission or AIRC) or cut the population wording.

claim: Hourly and casual workers may need 3-6 months of payslips; overtime and penalty income is often discounted by 20-50% in lending assessments.
why: These are lender-practice figures with no cited source on the page.

claim: Long service leave may qualify for concessional tax treatment.
why: This tax note is vague and hedged ('may'). The site's LSL calculator models the exact ATO rule: a flat 32% on genuine redundancy and pre-1993 or pre-1978 portions, otherwise marginal rate. The note should state that rule or link to the LSL calculator. It sits in a locked/strong context, so it was not edited in this pass.

claim: Ambulance Victoria Enterprise Agreement 2024 approved 14 February 2025 ([2025] FWCA 586) and operating from 21 February 2025
why: Not wrong-looking, but a reviewer should confirm the citation number and approval date against the FWC decision, because the sources entry pairs AE528036 with this decision number.

claim: Air Pilots Award 2020 is a 'Modern award in operation since 1 January 2010'.
why: 1 January 2010 is the start date of the earlier Air Pilots Award 2010. The 2020 award replaced it after the 4-yearly review, so the date may describe the predecessor award. The string is locked (prop:status), so it was not edited.

claim: Most contractors work 46-48 weeks (allowing for holidays)
why: This is a population claim with no source, in the weeks-per-year hint. It is locked by the dash rule, so I left it unchanged. It could be reworded as the page's own assumption (BILLABLE_WEEKS = 48 in contractor-pay-calculator-faqs.ts).

claim: The 2024 education staff agreement's nominal life runs about 36 months from 25 March 2024.
why: 'About 36 months' is a hedge on a fact the agreement states exactly. The page should give the agreement's actual nominal expiry date (around March 2027) instead of an approximation.

page: /public-service-pay-scales/qld/ao2/ to ao8/ (FAQ 'Is this what every QLD department pays...?')
claim: Most Queensland departments pay under the State Government Entities Certified Agreement 2023 (the core agreement).
why: This is a population claim ('most departments') with no figure or cited source on the page. The pilot lessons say such claims go here unless a source is cited. It is plausible, but it needs a source or a coverage list.

claim: Qualified boilermakers and electricians earn $85K to $120K; mining or oil and gas electricians $130K to $170K+; crane operators $100K to $150K+
why: Same problem: hard-coded, unsourced salary ranges presented as fact, and 'typically the highest-paid trades' is a population claim with no source.

claim: A contractor earning $78/hour commonly transitions to an employee salary of $100,000 to $105,000 per year.
why: Population claim ('commonly') with no source. The figures are typed, not computed.

claim: The NT agreement goes further than most: the parties agree an annual increment for teachers will only be withheld as an outcome of inability or discipline procedures under the PSEM Act.
why: Further than most compares the NT agreement with other agreements, but the page cites no source for that comparison. The FAQ at line 209 ("Unusually, ...") makes the same comparison. The clause itself is sourced. The comparison is not.

claim: Under the 2026-27 fortnightly tax table ... / What Changed in the Fortnightly Tax Table for 2026-27? / foreign-resident caption '2026-27'
why: The year '2026-27' is typed into the prose, the H2 (line 313) and a caption (line 230) instead of using PAYG_FINANCIAL_YEAR. These go stale at the next rollover, while the rest of the page updates itself.

claim: Most departments pay under the State Government Entities Certified Agreement 2023, so also check your department's own salary schedule.
why: This is a population claim ('most departments') with no figure, and the page does not cite a source for it. None of LEVEL_FACT_SOURCES names the SGE agreement. It also implies that the award table on the AO5 page is not what most Queensland public servants are paid, which the reviewer should confirm.

claim: 'most employers pass the FBT cost directly to the employee' and 'most novated leases on petrol cars use post-tax employee contributions'.
why: These are population claims with no figure and no cited source (checker warning). They could be reworded as mechanisms, for example 'when the employer passes the FBT cost on...' and 'novated leases on petrol cars use the employee contribution method...'. Owner decision.

claim: The public holiday pay guide has the full 14-award rate table
why: The award count is typed by hand on 8 pages. It should be calculated from the award public-holiday rate data so it cannot go stale.

claim: Weekend rates generally replace the shift loading rather than stacking on top of it, which is the single most common payslip misunderstanding in nursing.
why: 'Single most common payslip misunderstanding' is an unsourced superlative.

claim: public liability ($400 to $1,500 per year), professional indemnity ($500 to $2,000 per year), income protection ($800 to $2,500 per year); line 47: income protection costs 1 to 3% of income and replaces up to 70%
why: Premium ranges and the replacement ratio are hard-coded with no source cited on the page.

claim: A standard civil penalty under the Fair Work Act is up to 60 penalty units per contravention for individuals and 300 for companies, and serious contraventions attract up to ten times that.
why: The question is about underpayment. Since 1 January 2025 (Closing Loopholes Act), underpayment contraventions carry higher maximums (for example, the greater of 3x the underpayment or a multiple of the standard maximum for larger bodies corporate), and intentional wage underpayment is now a criminal offence. 60/300 units understates the exposure for this exact scenario.

claim: WA salaries are bigger, which pushes more of them into the 37% bracket.
why: This is a population claim with no source, and the 37% is typed rather than read from the bracket constants. The page's own example salary (WA AWOTE 2,227.40 x 52, about $115,825) sits in the 30% bracket, not the 37% one.

claim: Employers are more likely to offer packaging arrangements (super, novated leases, devices) to permanent salaried staff.
why: This is a population claim with no source on the page. It is now labelled 'Our view', but it still needs a source or should be cut. Any employee, including a permanent hourly employee, can salary sacrifice super.

claim: Employees paid fortnightly receive 26 deposits, which equates to the value of roughly 13 monthly payments across 12 calendar months. (Also: fortnightly pay produces 2 "extra" payments per year compared to a monthly cycle.)
why: 26 fortnightly pays of annual/26 add up to the same annual salary as 12 monthly pays, not 13. The 13-payment idea applies to halved mortgage repayments, not to pay. The '2 extra payments' only holds when compared with being paid twice a month (24 pays), not with a monthly cycle of 12. The same page's comparison paragraph says annual take-home is identical whatever the frequency.

claim: an employer who discovers a problem is almost always better off disclosing immediately and refining the numbers afterwards
why: This is an unlabelled editorial generalisation with 'almost always'. It should either be labelled as our view with the reason (the reduction decays from the payday) or have the absolute removed.

claim: Role salary range table (Driller $140,000 to $180,000 ... Labourer $80,000 to $110,000)
why: The figures are hard-coded and unsourced. The methodology attributes them to job advertisement data, but no date or source is given. The table supports the "well above $100,000 for most roles" claim on line 70.

claim: $268 a year, roughly $5 more per week; $10,800 in super on a $90,000 salary (line 493)
why: The figures are correct today (1% of $26,800, and 12% of $90,000), but they are typed in. They should come from the tax-bracket and SG constants so they cannot go stale.

claim: Public service payrolls usually pay fortnightly, which is why the schedules are published as fortnightly rates.
why: Most schedules in the data are annual salaries (APS, VPS, NSW, WA, Tas, ACT, NT pay points are stored as annual). Only the Queensland award states the fortnightly rate is the binding rate (qld.ts:78). The causal claim looks too wide for every service.

claim: The second bracket fell from 16% to 15% ... up to $268 less
why: The figures are correct ($26,800 x 1% = $268), but they are hard-coded and do not come from the 2025-26 and 2026-27 bracket constants.

claim: 'Most {j.shortName} departments pay under their own agreement'
why: This is a population claim with no figure or cited source. It renders on every caveated level page. It needs a source, or it should be restated as a fact about the named agreements.

claim: Most young workers are covered by an award, which sets its own percentages against the award rate instead.
why: Population claim with no figure or cited source on the page.

claim: most staff are paid a higher Contract Rate (repeated at line 169: 'Most staff are paid a Contract Rate above the base rate')
why: This is a claim about how many staff are paid above base, and nothing cited supports it. Clause 1.6 says only that the Contract Rate is at least the base rate. It does not say how many staff are paid more than base.

claim: Most airline pilots (at Qantas, Virgin Australia, Jetstar, Rex and regional carriers) are paid under their airline's enterprise agreement, which pays well above these minimums
why: This claims a share of a population ('most') and an amount ('well above') with no figure, and the page cites no source for it. The sources list only covers the Air Pilots Award.

claim: The table titled 'Paramedic entry level and Paramedic Level 1 (Table 1A)', whose intro covers Trainee Paramedics, Paramedic Interns and qualified Paramedics, also includes rows such as 'Paramedic Educator (Level 4, Band 2, Increment 2)'.
why: The table title and intro look narrower than the rows the table actually lists. The owner should check whether Level 2 to Level 4 rows belong in this scale or whether the title needs widening. This is a structure question, not a text edit.

claim: The running cost budget is set based on estimated annual kilometres (typically 15,000 to 20,000 km)
why: A 'typical' kilometre range with no source is a claim about a population. It is a hard-coded figure that does not come from a constant.

claim: Most FIFO jobs in mining, oil and gas and construction pay an hourly rate set by an enterprise agreement. ... Many agreements average the 38-hour week across the roster cycle
why: Population claims ('most', 'many') with no figure and no cited source on the page.

claim: PAYG Withholding is the single largest deduction on every Australian payslip.
why: It overclaims. An employee under the tax-free threshold who claims it has nil PAYG withheld, and a large salary sacrifice can exceed PAYG. This is a protected first sentence, so I left it unchanged.

claim: Tasmania Police Recruitment says a first-year Constable on Level 1 ($73,518) with the 28% shift penalty allowance has a gross salary of $94,109.
why: $73,518 x 1.28 = $94,103.04, not $94,109. The $6 gap may be in Tasmania Police Recruitment's own published figure, or the figure may have been copied wrong. Check it against the Benefits page before it is quoted.

claim: Most shop assistants are level 1.
why: Population claim with no figure or cited source on the page.

claim: LITO is {formatAUD(LITO.maxOffset)} up to $37,500 and tapers after that
why: $37,500 is typed in, though LITO.fullOffsetCeiling already holds it (also LITO_ROWS on line 58 uses a literal 37_500).

claim: On a {gross gain} gain with ${formatAUD(100_000)} of other income ...
why: The other-income figure is typed as the literal 100_000 in the answer rather than read from the EXAMPLE input object. It would drift if the example's otherIncome changed.

claim: Level 5 works under broad direction with responsibility for others' work (A.7.1)
why: The file's own header note (lines 19-21) records A.7.1 as 'broad guidance and may hold relevant post-secondary qualifications'. It does not mention responsibility for others' work, so the coverage paragraph may not match the award text.

claim: The Commission could complete it over two more reviews or spread it further
why: This conflicts with the lead and key facts ("over three stages", "Total phase-out stages: 3"). It also guesses at a future FWC decision without citing a source. Confirm the number of stages against the decision and remove one of the two claims.

claim: Applying for a TFN at a post office or online takes approximately 10 business days.
why: WHMs (foreign passport holders) apply online, and the ATO says to allow up to 28 days. The post office option is for Australian residents.

claim: Payroll tax is the largest variable on-cost
why: The workers compensation table on the same page shows rates of 3% to 7% (construction) and 10%+ (mining). Those can exceed the VIC payroll tax rate, so calling payroll tax the largest is not true for every industry.

claim: Employee contributions are the most common strategy for reducing FBT on car fringe benefits and novated leases.
why: This population claim has no cited source.

claim: The ACT reaches the entitlement fastest of any jurisdiction: 6.0667 weeks of paid leave after just 7 years
why: Victoria also qualifies at 7 years with 6.0667 weeks (vic takeAfterYears 7, weeksAtQualifying 6.0667), so 'fastest of any jurisdiction' is a tie. It now contradicts the edited VIC summary ('shares the shortest qualifying period ... with the ACT'). The ACT is only uniquely faster on the pro-rata trigger (5 years, shared with NSW).

claim: Many awards pay it; the National Employment Standards do not.
why: A population claim ('many awards') with no source on the page. It is true in practice (17.5% annual leave loading is common), but the brief sends unsourced population claims to review.

claim: Many lenders, landlords, and government agencies accept the NOA as proof of income... Banks commonly request your last 2 NOAs when assessing home loan applications.
why: This is a population claim with no source. Lenders ask for 2 NOAs mainly from self-employed borrowers, not from PAYG employees.

claim: Allow 3-5 business days for bank transfers to process.
why: This is a processing-time figure with no source. It is a convenience estimate rather than a rule, and nothing on the page cites the ATO for it.

claim: Allowances cited as 'Appendix 2 Part 2' (lines 113, 230, 248)
why: The file header (line 5) cites the wages as Appendix 2A Part 1 and the allowances as Part 2 of the same appendix (Appendix 2A Part 2).

claim: People with more than one job, investment income with no tax withheld, or a study loan are the most likely to get a bill.
why: This is a population claim ('most likely') and the page cites no source for it. The mechanism is sound, but the ranking is unsourced.

claim: The difference between column 2 and column 3 is the single most common cause.
why: This is a claim about which cause is most common, with no source cited. The brief says such claims go to factQuestions. It also comes after the line that says to check the TFN declaration only if nothing else explains the gap, so the two sentences point in different directions.

claim: Credit cards, car loans and personal loans all cost more, so they come first.
why: This is prioritisation advice stated as a rule. It gives no figure or source to show that all three cost more than the {HECS_HELP.indexationRate} indexation, and the page's AUDIT does not allow labelled opinion. The owner should decide whether to keep it, cite typical rates, or reword it as labelled guidance.

claim: 'Many Melbourne Cup Day workers are in hospitality: pubs, clubs and restaurants run big days around the race.'
why: This is a population claim ('many') with no figure, and the page cites no source for it. I kept the sentence because it is the reason the calculator defaults to hospitality, but it needs a source or a rewording.

claim: An experienced clinical psychologist working as a senior clinician or specialist would typically fit Level 2 ($51.19 to $52.19 an hour) or, as an advanced clinician, Level 3 ($52.19).
why: This is not a wrong figure. The answer hedges a classification rule with 'would typically', yet coverage[2] defines Level 2 as a senior clinician or specialist. The string is locked (it is an argument to hpssOct2026Occupation), so this pass could not tighten it. Level 2.2 and Level 3 both being $52.19 matches HPSS_OCT_2026_SENIOR.

claim: The government has said it will complete a review of the exemption by mid-2027.
why: This is hard-coded prose, but the same value exists as EV_EXEMPTION.reviewDue. With the review date close, check its status as at Oct 2026.

claim: The 15% rate was introduced in January 2017 ... has remained at 15% since the 2017-18 financial year.
why: Internal inconsistency: a 1 January 2017 start falls in FY2016-17, not 2017-18.

claim: Enterprise agreement site allowances can be 'significantly higher' than the award amounts on major commercial and infrastructure projects.
why: This is a population or comparison claim with no source or figure. The same claim appears as 'often much higher' in construction-trades-pay-faqs.ts line 38.

claim: That is why the APS-wide percentile ranges overlap: an EL 1 at the bottom of the band earns less than an APS 6 at the top of theirs in the same agency.
why: The page's own data contradicts this. The APSC APS 6 95th percentile ($115,199) is below the EL 1 5th percentile ($124,861), so those ranges do not overlap. Treasury EL 1.1 ($137,301) is above Treasury APS 6.4 ($127,521), and the EL 1 threshold minimum ($121,755) is above the APS 6 threshold maximum ($111,701). Only the lower levels overlap (APS 3/4 and APS 4/5). The sentence needs to be rewritten

claim: Most residents pay an extra 2% of their whole taxable income
why: This is a population claim with no figure or source on the page. It is probably right because low-income earners are exempt or pay a reduced levy, but no source on the page backs "most".

claim: updated personal caps aren't expected to display in ATO online services until 13 July 2026
why: Stale future tense: it is now October 2026. If the ATO did display updated caps from 13 July 2026, the sentence should state that in the past tense; the key facts row (line 18) says 'From 13 July 2026'.

claim: The National Employment Standards (NES) define maximum ordinary hours as 38 hours per week for full-time employees.
why: NES s62 sets maximum weekly hours (38 plus reasonable additional hours), not "maximum ordinary hours". This is a wording precision question; I left it unchanged.

claim: Salon Saturdays are 133%, "not the 125% most awards use"
why: This is a comparative claim about other awards with no count or source. It is probably true of the retail and hospitality awards on this site, but nothing on the page supports it.

claim: WA moves two holidays that most of the country holds on fixed dates: Labour Day falls in early March
why: Labour Day has no common fixed date across Australia. VIC and TAS hold it in March, QLD and NT in May, and NSW, ACT and SA in October, so 'most of the country holds on fixed dates' is wrong for Labour Day.

claim: Self-employed plumbers and electricians 'may gross $150,000–$250,000'. Boilermakers and electricians earn the most because of mining and heavy industry demand.
why: No source is cited for either the figure or the cause. The same figures appear in construction-trades-pay-faqs.ts line 26.

claim: The Department of Education's public rates page still shows 2022 rates and says it is under review.
why: A point-in-time claim about a third-party page, read on 24 September 2026. It goes stale once the department updates the page, so it needs a re-check date or a 'when we checked' framing.

claim: 'Most Australians are affected by the first and third' (line 9), 'For most workers, this is the single biggest practical change' (line 30), 'a small share of super members, concentrated in large self-managed super funds' (line 41), 'These increases give most super members more room' (line 64)
why: These are population claims with no figure or cited source. A Treasury or ATO count of people above $3m TSB, or of SG-eligible employees, would make them checkable. Otherwise they should be reworded as conditions.

claim: notShown lists 'Aged care enrolled nurse rates', but the enrolled nurse section (line 136) does show the aged care enrolled nurse (supervising) weekly and hourly rate from EN_AGED.
why: The page contradicts itself: one aged care EN rate is shown, so 'not shown' is only partly true.

claim: Schedule B is the stream most people mean by "SCHADS rates" ... and most disability support work delivered outside the home.
why: Two population claims ('most people', 'most disability support work') with no figure or cited source. Line 376 also says disability support sits in Schedule B or, when delivered in the home, Schedule E, which makes 'most' look looser than the page's own rule.

claim: Most employees are covered by an award, which sets its own minimum for each classification.
why: This is a population claim with no figure and no source on the page. ABS Employee Earnings and Hours data puts award-only employees at roughly a quarter of the workforce.
